questions.question: Which statement best captures the lesson's core document-modeling invariant?
options: Every relationship should be embedded to avoid joins
Data that must change atomically should live in one bounded document; cross-document consistency needs an explicit mechanism
Flexible schema removes the need for validation
Every collection should use the same document shape
questions.explanation: Single-document writes are atomic, so the document is the natural consistency boundary. Growth and independent ownership still determine whether embedding remains safe.

questions.question: A post can receive an unbounded number of independently moderated comments. Which starting model is safest?
options: Embed every comment forever in the post document
Store comments as referenced documents and page them with a suitable index
Put all comments for the site in one document
Disable schema validation
questions.explanation: The relationship grows without a useful bound and each comment has an independent lifecycle, so references avoid a hot, ever-growing parent document.

questions.question: In a three-voting-member replica set, what does write concern majority normally require?
options: Acknowledgment from the primary only
Acknowledgment at the majority commit boundary, normally two voting data-bearing members
Acknowledgment from all clients
A read from every secondary
questions.explanation: A majority of three is two. Waiting for that boundary reduces rollback exposure but can increase latency or reject progress when a majority is unavailable.

questions.question: A majority write times out. What may the application safely conclude?
options: The write definitely did not reach any member
The write definitely committed and can be repeated without checking
The required acknowledgment was not observed in time; the application must reconcile by idempotency key or authoritative state
Every secondary rolled back
questions.explanation: A timeout describes the missing acknowledgment, not definitive absence of the write. Retrying a non-idempotent business action can duplicate it.

questions.question: Which compound-index order follows equality-sort-range for a query filtering tenant and status, sorting newest first, and bounding amount?
options: { amount: 1, createdAt: -1, tenantId: 1, status: 1 }
{ tenantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1, amount: 1 }
{ createdAt: -1, amount: 1 }
{ amount: 1 }
questions.explanation: Equality fields lead, the sort field follows when preserving index order is the priority, and the range field comes after them. Explain output must still validate the choice.

questions.question: Why can a monotonically increasing shard key create a hot shard?
options: New values tend to land on the current edge chunk, concentrating writes
MongoDB cannot index numeric fields
Replica sets reject ordered keys
It forces every query to use GridFS
questions.explanation: Sequential new values converge on one range edge until chunks split and move. Hashed distribution can spread writes but trades away range locality.

questions.question: A secondary serves reads with local concern while it is 12 seconds behind. What guarantee should the product expose?
options: The read is always the newest globally committed value
The read may be stale by the observed replication lag and may include state not guaranteed against rollback
The read is linearizable
The read automatically waits for the primary
questions.explanation: Secondary-local reads favor availability or locality over freshness and durable commit guarantees. The application must tolerate and communicate that bounded staleness.

questions.question: Which evidence best demonstrates recoverability?
options: Three replicas report healthy
A recent backup file exists
A representative restore completed within the objective, including index build, oplog catch-up, validation, and cutover
The primary has low CPU
questions.explanation: Replication copies application mistakes, and backup existence does not prove recovery. A measured restore exercise validates the complete recovery path.
